A hybrid semi-empirical model was developed that relates the radar backscattering coefficient to soil moisture and surface roughness.
The semi-empirical model was extended to be fully polarimetric by incorporating the phase difference statistics between co- and cross-polarized radar returns.
A general scattering model for grass blades of arbitrary cross-section was developed and incorporated into a first-order random media model for vegetation-covered surfaces.
A new polarimetric calibration technique was developed that characterizes the complete radar polarization distortion matrix using a sphere measured over the entire antenna mainlobe.

Three different numerical approaches were developed to simulate scattering from rough surfaces, including methods to eliminate edge effects, handle inhomogeneous dielectrics, and improve computational efficiency.
A prototype soil moisture probe based on microstrip resonators was developed that is more accurate and convenient to use than traditional coaxial probes.
A fully polarimetric bistatic scattering system was designed and tested to operate in the 8.5-10 GHz and 34-35 GHz frequency ranges.
Extensive ground-truth data and polarimetric backscatter measurements were collected over a wheat field during the entire growing season, showing significant backscatter sensitivity to soil moisture.

Key students included Yisok Oh, Roger Dean De Roo, James Norman Stiles, and Tsen Chie Chiu, with dissertation topics covering polarimetric backscattering, bistatic scattering, vegetation scattering models, and scattering from rough surfaces with vegetation.
The research was supported by the Terrestrial Ecology Program of NASA Headquarters and was conducted at the Radiation Laboratory of the University of Michigan.
The research period covered in this final report was from May 1993 to October 1996.
The main objective of the investigation was the characterization of soil moisture using imaging radars.
The research involved theoretical, numerical, and experimental aspects of electromagnetic scattering from natural surfaces, with a focus on remote sensing of soil moisture.
A level-1 SAR image classifier was developed to identify statistically homogeneous distributed targets in the imaged scene, which was important for the soil moisture estimation objective.
An in situ and in vivo vegetation dielectric measurement technique was developed using a waveguide method.
